text:
Level Measurement

 Servo Level Gauge Working Principle Explained

 A servo gauge doesn't just hang a displacer in a tank and read a number.

 It's a continuously self correcting weighing machine, chasing the liquid surface thousands of times a day to keep one small object exactly balanced.

 
 Null-Balance Control 
 Live Density Calculator 
 Servo vs Radar Compared 
 




 A servo level gauge working principle relies on continuously rebalancing a small displacer against buoyant force, using a servo motor to track the liquid surface to within a fraction of a millimeter.


 Picture a standard displacer level transmitter , but instead of hanging passively on a spring, the displacer rides on a wire. A motor actively winds that wire in and out.


 
 
 
 The gauge never lets the displacer drift out of balance for long. The instant buoyancy shifts, the motor repositions the displacer to restore the exact same reference weight.


 
 
 Image credit: Honeywell (Enraf Servo 954 Tank Gauge)

 The 5 Core Parts of a Servo Level Gauge

 Every servo gauge, regardless of brand, is built around the same five working parts.


 
 
 1

 Displacer
 A small, dense object lowered into the liquid, denser than the process fluid so it never floats freely.


 

 
 2

 Measuring Wire and Drum
 A fine stainless steel wire winds onto a precision grooved drum that tracks exact displacer position.


 

 
 3

 Magnetic Coupling
 Outer magnets on the drum and inner magnets on the motor transfer torque without any shaft seal penetrating the housing.


 

 
 4

 Hall Effect Sensors
 Typically five sensors detect tiny changes in magnetic flux as buoyancy shifts the torque on the coupling.


 

 
 5

 Servo Motor and Control Loop
 Drives the drum to raise or lower the displacer, continuously restoring the reference apparent weight.


 




 Servo Gauge vs Static Displacer Transmitter

 Both rely on Archimedes' principle, but one sits still while the other actively hunts for balance.


 
 
 ⚖

 Static Displacer (Torque Tube)

 Stays at a fixed position, sensing a change in apparent weight as level moves past it. Simple, no moving control loop.

 Passive, continuous range

 

 
 🔄

 Servo Gauge

 Actively repositions the displacer to stay exactly at the surface, using a closed control loop for extreme precision.

 Active, null-balance tracking

 Advertisement 
 

 



 

 How Null-Balance Control Actually Works

 
 Null-balance means the gauge always drives the error back to zero, rather than measuring a steady state deflection.

 
 Setpoint: a fixed reference apparent weight for the displacer

 Error too low: buoyancy increased, motor lowers the displacer

 Error too high: buoyancy decreased, motor raises the displacer



 
 The wire position, not the displacer's weight reading, is what actually gets converted into the level measurement. Position is precise. Weight alone would drift with vibration and friction.

 Why servo gauges reach sub-millimeter accuracy






 Buoyancy and Density Formulas

 The same buoyant force math applies here, but a servo gauge can also solve it in reverse to determine liquid density.


 
 Buoyant Force and Density from Immersion Change

 Fb = ρ x g x A x h
ρ = ΔF / (g x A x Δh)

 
 Where ρ = liquid density, g = 9.81 m/s2, A = displacer cross section

 ΔF = change in apparent weight, Δh = change in immersion depth


 Example: A = 0.0008 m2, ΔF = 0.04 N, Δh = 0.05 m

 ρ = 0.04 / (9.81 x 0.0008 x 0.05) = approximately 1019 kg/m3
 




 Servo Gauge vs Radar Gauge

 Servo remains common in existing terminals, but radar is now the default choice for new installations.


 
 
 Property Servo Gauge Radar Gauge 
 
 
 Moving parts Yes, wire, drum, motor, displacer None in the measurement path 

 Typical accuracy ±0.4 to 0.7 mm Comparable or better, no wear-related drift 

 Density and interface measurement Native capability Requires added sensors or hybrid setup 

 Maintenance Higher, mechanical wear over years Lower, largely maintenance free 

 
 



 Where Servo Level Gauges Are Used

 
 ⚖
 Custody Transfer
 OIML R85 and API 3.1B certified fiscal measurement.


 🚛
 Crude Oil Storage
 Bulk terminal inventory management and reconciliation.


 💧
 Interface Measurement
 Oil-water interface tracking in separator and storage tanks.


 📊
 Density Profiling
 Measuring density at multiple depths in a stratified tank.


 ⛽
 Refined Products
 Light and middle distillate storage and blending operations.


 ⚠
 Overfill Prevention
 SIL 2/3 rated independent high level protection.





 Why Wire Winding Layers Affect Accuracy

 A grooved drum sounds simple, but multi-layer winding introduces a subtle error source engineers should know about.

 As the wire builds up in layers, the effective drum radius changes slightly with each layer. The same motor rotation now represents a different length of wire feed.

 High end servo gauges compensate for this electronically, tracking exactly which layer the wire sits on. Older or poorly maintained units can drift in accuracy specifically because this compensation degrades over time.

 Do's and Don'ts of Servo Gauge Operation

 
 
 ✓ Do

 
 Inspect the measuring wire regularly for wear or corrosion

 Verify density readings against a lab sample periodically

 Keep the displacer clean, since sticky product can bias the weight reading

 Confirm magnetic coupling integrity during scheduled maintenance

 
 

 
 ✗ Don't

 
 Ignore repeated fault alarms on the servo motor drive

 Assume density accuracy matches level accuracy in every service

 Let foam or vapor buildup interfere with displacer contact detection
